Assignment 07 / Sculpting for Design

Carving in Plaster of Paris

An expressive face and a patterned pillar, carved from Plaster of Paris.

Plaster of Paris · Carving

Two plaster studies explore how a small number of incisions can suggest an expression or establish a repeated pattern. The material also introduces a practical lesson in timing: plaster becomes more resistant to carving as it hardens.

01

An expression in the eyes

For the smaller plaster carving, Medha wanted to create a face. She drew on manga she had read as a child, particularly the way a close view of the eyes can communicate a full expression through eye angles and eyebrows.

The carving translates that idea into a compact three-dimensional object. Shallow cuts establish the features, while the different views reveal how those incisions sit on the curved plaster surface.

02

A lesson in timing

The pillar explores simple carved patterns. Here the material also introduced a practical difficulty: Medha waited too long after setting the plaster, and it became hard to carve.

She remained satisfied with the result. In her reflection, the depth created by subtraction gives the surface an effect she compares to whittled wood. The repeating marks make the cuts themselves part of the piece’s character.

03

Expression and pattern

The smaller face and the taller pillar use the same subtractive process for different purposes. One concentrates on eye angles and eyebrows; the other develops a sequence of geometric and curved marks around a larger form.

Together, the photographs show how carved depth changes a surface. The incisions remain visible as physical cuts, with light and shadow helping to describe their shape.

04

Learning from the material

Waiting too long after setting made the pillar difficult to carve. Medha’s reflection makes that difficulty part of the project: the material’s changing hardness affected the making process and the character of the finished surface.

She remained satisfied with the result, particularly the whittled-wood effect created by the depth of the cuts. The project records both the finished forms and the practical experience of working with plaster.

The original pages.

This shared submission documents the plaster face and pillar on pages 3–4; the foam study has its own project page.
